It’s a production charged with adolescent passion and buzzing with fresh insights.
This is a richly emotional, brilliantly intelligent take on a classic – one that'll plunge a knife into your heart so skilfully that you hardly notice the pain.

Like Robert Icke’s production, she conveys something essential about the action of this romance – its hysteria and its precariousness – yet detracts from that truth with hyper activity, multiple underlinings.
What makes the production effective, ultimately, in spite of the overbearing directorial stamp, are the two central performances.

Icke’s production is intermittently revelatory, yet also oddly obstructive: a sunless vision of fair Verona with an almost constant backing track you’d normally associate with an aromatherapy massage at a posh spa.
With Sadie Sink as Juliet and Noah Jupe as Romeo, this is a production that understands exactly what makes Shakespeare's tragedy work, and then finds ways to make it hit even harder.
It’s clever and original, making this an utterly thrilling vision.
With Sink, Icke has struck gold.
You're reminded afresh in Icke's empathic vision of the play that its collective emphasis on banishment might as well be a more polite way of referencing death.
If it isn’t quite up there with Icke’s best, that’s only because he has set the bar so high.
Everything good about Icke’s “Romeo and Juliet” is bound up in sincerity and sentiment.
Fortunately, the play's second act packs a gut-punch that almost makes one forget about the discordant way the first ended.
In doing so, it makes the most famous play in history feel brand new.
A gem of a show and an inventive and insightful adaptation of a classic.
In this, he succeeds on a monumental scale.
Noah Jupe, 21, and Sadie Sink, 23, make for convincing teenagers, conveying both instant infatuation and terrible judgement.
Overall, Icke has created an extremely impressive and contemporary revival of Shakespeare’s tragic love story.
It’s inventive, surprising, and utterly compelling.

cn.t: Icke's time-bending production wins praise for its urgency and emotional power, with Sink delivering a standout performance. Critics laud the fresh approach and youthful energy, though some find the conceptual devices gimmicky.
